did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with a plea for protection: David turns to the LORD because he has chosen to take refuge in and trust him.
Did you know? In this verse, the psalmist acknowledges the LORD as his master and emphasizes that his goodness cannot add anything to God; rather, it expresses his devotion to him.
Did you know? The psalmist describes the holy and noble people of the land as those in whom he delights; this distinguishes the company of those who worship the LORD from that of idol worshipers.
Did you know? The psalmist declares that he will not take part in idol worship: he will not pour out their drink offerings or speak their names with his lips.
Did you know? The expression “the portion of my inheritance and my cup” presents the LORD as the psalmist’s portion and destiny, while “you hold my lot” emphasizes the LORD’s support of him.
Did you know? Using images of measuring lines, inheritance, and property, the psalmist describes his destiny as good, pleasant, and beautiful in his eyes.
Did you know? The psalmist blesses the LORD for his counsel and adds that even at night he receives inward correction or guidance, as it says: “even at night my heart instructs me.”
Did you know? Setting the LORD always before him is connected to the psalmist’s stability: because the LORD is at his right hand, he declares that he will not be shaken.
Did you know? In this verse, joy spreads from the heart to the glory and the body: “my heart is glad,” “my glory rejoices,” and “my flesh also rests secure.”
Did you know? The psalmist expresses confidence that the LORD will not abandon his soul to Sheol or let his faithful one see the pit; this is a declaration of hope for deliverance and life.
Did you know? The psalm’s conclusion presents the LORD as a guide: he makes known “the path of life,” and in his presence there is fullness of joy and eternal pleasures.
